meta.description: Rules for removing the stock shapes (closers, contrast pairs, framing beats) and for breaking up runs of one construction. Sentence length follows the content.
meta.usage: Second pass of the application protocol, after lexical. Call humanizer_get_structural_patterns to retrieve.
meta.research_basis: Ardeshirifar (2025) showed human texts have wider sentence-length distributions with higher standard deviation. Muñoz-Ortiz et al. (2024) documented POS distribution differences across six LLMs. Terčon & Dobrovoljc (2025) survey synthesized 44 studies on syntactic complexity, sentence length, and structural patterns.

sentence_length.ai_pattern: AI text concentrates around shorter, more uniform sentence lengths. The standard deviation of sentence length is consistently lower in AI text than in human text.
sentence_length.human_pattern: Human writers demonstrate greater variability: wider distribution, higher standard deviation. Sentences range from fragments to long multi-clause constructions within the same passage.

rules.rule: Let sentence length follow the content.
rules.guidance: A sentence runs as long as the thought it carries. Do not plan a mix of short and long sentences for each paragraph. Fragments and one-line questions written for rhythm read as a model's cadence, so leave them out. Some paragraphs read evenly; that is fine.

rules.rule: Keep a fragment only where the content calls for one.
rules.guidance: A fragment can answer a question someone asked, or render speech. Placed after a long sentence to create a beat, it reads as performed rhythm; a run of such beats is a known model tell. When a fragment is there for effect, fold it into the sentence before it.

rules.rule: Allow long sentences when the thought demands it.
rules.guidance: AI tends to break complex thoughts into multiple short sentences. Sometimes a single long sentence with embedded clauses, parenthetical asides, or subordinate constructions reads more naturally than three short ones. Do not use em-dashes to extend sentences (see absolute_rules AR-002); use commas, semicolons, parentheses, or restructured subordinate clauses.

rules.rule: Let paragraph length follow the content.
rules.guidance: A point that needs one sentence gets a one-sentence paragraph; a point that needs six sentences gets six. Model drafts tend to keep paragraphs at one length and to set a single line apart for impact when its point belongs in the paragraph before.

rules.rule: Do not aim for a sentence-length average or spread.
rules.guidance: Mean sentence length does not distinguish model text from human text. The checker reports the spread (standard deviation) as a diagnostic. When it reads low, look for a run of sentences built on one shape and recombine or split them by meaning. Do not add short sentences to move the number (see caveats.sentence_length_mean_not_a_signal).

syntactic_variety.ai_pattern: AI text shows more rigid, repetitive sentence structure. It favors Subject-Verb-Object order, overuses auxiliary verbs and copula constructions, and produces more subordinate clauses and verb phrases relative to human text. Syntactic depth remains stable across sentences.
syntactic_variety.human_pattern: Human writers demonstrate flexibility, tailoring sentence structure based on communicative goals such as clarity, emphasis, or engagement. Syntactic depth fluctuates across adjacent sentences.

rules.rule: Use a simple declarative where the next point is simple.
rules.guidance: A complex sentence ('While the data suggests one thing, the experience on the ground, which few researchers have examined closely, points in another direction') can be followed by a simple one when the next fact is simple ('Two of the three sites reported the same drop.'). The simple sentence carries a fact; a short abstract verdict in that slot is a model habit.

rules.rule: Front-load modifiers occasionally.
rules.guidance: Instead of always 'The system processes data efficiently,' sometimes write 'Efficiently, the system processes data.' Vary which elements get emphasis through position.

rules.rule: Use passive voice selectively.
rules.guidance: Instruction-tuned models use the agentless passive less often than human writers do, so do not strip passives to sound human. Use the passive where the object matters more than the actor ('The bridge was closed for two days'), and the active where the actor is the news. Human writers are uneven here; an even, all-active surface is its own pattern.
rules.history: Corrected 2026-10-30: instruction-tuned models use the agentless passive LESS than humans, not more (GPT-4o at about half the human rate, Reinhart et al., PNAS 2025).

rules.rule: Keep a sentence-initial 'And' or 'But' where the link is additive or contrastive.
rules.guidance: A sentence can open with 'And' when it adds to the one before, or 'But' when it turns against it. Both are ordinary English, and editing them out to sound formal is a model habit. Do not add one to change the rhythm.

rules.rule: Keep a question the source asks.
rules.guidance: A question belongs where the writer or the source puts one to the reader or to the argument. A one-line question placed to break a run of statements reads as a model's cadence.

rules.rule: Vary clause ordering to shift emphasis.
rules.guidance: Human writers reorder clauses to put emphasis where they want it. 'Despite the cost, they went ahead' vs. 'They went ahead, despite the cost': same information, different emphasis. AI tends to use one ordering pattern consistently.

rules.rule: Prefer verb-led constructions over noun-chain constructions.
rules.guidance: AI builds sentences around noun phrases: 'The analysis of the data revealed...' Humans build them around verbs: 'We analyzed the data and found...' When you see 'the [noun] of [noun]' twice in one sentence, restructure around the verb. See lexical_patterns.nominalization for the full list.

rules.rule: Reduce that-clause subjects.
rules.guidance: AI produces sentences like 'That the system performed well is noteworthy' or 'That climate change affects agriculture is well documented.' Human writers almost never start sentences this way. Restructure: 'The system performed well, which is worth noting' or 'Climate change clearly affects agriculture.' Move the that-clause to the end or eliminate it.

rules.rule: Cut trailing present participial clauses.
rules.guidance: AI appends '-ing' tails that add interpretation without new information: 'The policy was updated in March, reflecting a shift in organizational priorities and underscoring the need for ongoing adaptation.' Human writers either commit to the interpretation in a separate sentence or drop it. If the participial clause can be deleted without losing a fact, delete it.

rules.rule: Replace periphrastic verb constructions with direct verbs.
rules.guidance: AI favors multi-word verb phrases over single direct verbs. 'is able to process' → 'processes'. 'has been shown to improve' → 'improves'. 'can be used to generate' → 'generates'. 'is designed to facilitate' → 'helps'. Audit sentences for auxiliary verb chains (is/are/was/were/has/have/can/could + past participle or infinitive) and ask if a single verb would work.

rules.rule: Reduce copula constructions ('is', 'are', 'was') when a stronger verb is available.
rules.guidance: AI defaults to 'X is a Y that Z' structure. 'The platform is a tool that enables collaboration' → 'The platform lets teams collaborate.' Not every copula should be replaced. When three sentences in a row use 'is/are/was' as the main verb, check whether one of them has a stronger verb available.

punctuation_diversity.ai_pattern: AI text uses a less varied set of punctuation marks, with commas and periods accounting for most cases. Historically, AI used fewer question marks, parentheses, semicolons, and colons compared to human text. It uses more periods and single quotes. Note: em-dashes are NOT a human signal in current detector landscapes; see AR-002 in absolute_rules.
punctuation_diversity.human_pattern: Human writers choose each mark for the sentence in front of them, so parentheses, semicolons and colons turn up where a sentence calls for one. Keep the source's choices and do not vary punctuation for its own sake.

rules.rule: Absolute: never use em-dashes (—). See absolute_rules AR-002 for the full directive.
rules.guidance: Em-dashes are one of the most reliable AI tells in current reader and detector environments. For parenthetical asides, use commas ('The project, which started as a side experiment, became the main product'), parentheses ('The project (originally a side experiment) became the main product'), or restructure into two sentences. Between two independent clauses, use a period, or a semicolon when the clauses are closely joined; a comma there is a comma splice (see absolute_rules AR-003). If the second clause carries the point, lead with it. When revising source text that already contains em-dashes, replace every one without changing the meaning.

rules.rule: Use semicolons to connect related independent clauses.
rules.guidance: A semicolon joins two independent clauses that belong together, where a period would separate them more than the thought does. Never join them with a bare comma.

rules.rule: Use colons to introduce lists and definitions.
rules.guidance: A colon introduces a list or a definition ('Bring three things: a pen, your ID and the signed form.'). Do not use a colon to stage a reveal, where the words before it only set up the point after it; state the point.

rules.rule: Use parentheses for asides.
rules.guidance: Parenthetical asides (like this one) let a writer add context without breaking the main sentence. Use parentheses or commas for the aside; never em-dashes (see AR-002).

rules.rule: Keep the source's punctuation choices where several are valid.
rules.guidance: Human writers are inconsistent in the CHOICE of punctuation. They may use Oxford commas in one paragraph and drop them in another, or lean on semicolons in one section and parentheses elsewhere. Where the source drifts like this, keep its choices and do not standardize them, and do not add drift to text that has none. Drift applies only where multiple valid options exist (Oxford comma on/off, semicolon vs. period to join related clauses, parens vs. commas for an aside). It is never license to drop required punctuation, omit terminal marks, or use a mark incorrectly; punctuation must always be grammatically correct (see absolute_rules AR-003). The other exception is em-dashes (see AR-002): never use them, regardless of section.

rules.rule: Use ellipses very sparingly.
rules.guidance: An occasional ellipsis (' ... ') can indicate trailing thought, but overuse is its own AI signal in some models. One per document maximum in professional prose.

n_gram_patterns.ai_pattern: AI text shows higher frequencies for word n-grams of order 3+, meaning it repeats the same multi-word phrases more than human writers. LLMs also repeat longer part-of-speech sequences more frequently. For n-grams of order 6+, LLMs produce more novel combinations than humans, while for shorter n-grams they produce fewer novel combinations.
rewriting_guidance: Check for repeated 3–4 word phrases across the document. If the same phrase appears more than twice and does not name a thing, rephrase at least one instance. A phrase that names a thing keeps one wording throughout, so keep the source's term.
Avoid formulaic sentence openings. If three sentences start with 'This [noun]...' or 'The [noun]...', rewrite at least one with a different construction.

enumeration_patterns.ai_pattern: AI over-relies on parallel list structures within prose. Three-item lists in parallel form ('X, Y, and Z') appear at a much higher rate than in human text. AI also produces more phrasal coordination and stacks multiple coordinate structures in the same sentence.
enumeration_patterns.human_pattern: Human writers embed items in flowing prose rather than listing them. When they do list, the items are often different lengths, and they vary between two-item, three-item, and four-item constructions. They also use subordination rather than coordination to relate ideas.

rules.rule: Vary list lengths. Do not default to three items.
rules.guidance: If three consecutive sentences or paragraphs contain three-item lists, rewrite at least one. Sometimes two items is enough. Sometimes four is better. Sometimes the 'list' should just be a sentence: 'The main benefit is speed, though reliability matters too.'

rules.rule: Embed items in prose rather than enumerating them.
rules.guidance: 'The platform offers analytics, reporting, and dashboards' → 'The platform's main draw is its analytics; the reporting fills in the gaps, and the dashboards are mostly for client presentations.' Items gain texture when they're described, not listed.

rules.rule: Replace coordination with subordination where one item matters more.
rules.guidance: 'The team designed, developed, and deployed the system' → 'The team designed and deployed the system; developing it took most of the time.' Subordination signals that the writer has judged the relative importance of items, which AI rarely does.

enumeration_patterns.research_basis: Strübbe et al. (2025) and Wu (2025) both find higher coordination and enumeration in AI text. Anti-pattern AP-011 addresses the 'rule of three' specifically; this rule generalizes the principle.

dependency_proximity.description: Human languages naturally minimize the distance between syntactically related words due to working memory constraints. LLMs do this less effectively than humans, producing word orders where modifiers, objects, and their governors are farther apart than a human writer would place them.
dependency_proximity.ai_pattern: AI may produce sentences where the subject and verb are separated by long modifying phrases, or where relative pronouns are distant from their antecedents. The sentence is grammatical but feels slightly harder to parse than it should.
dependency_proximity.human_pattern: Human writers intuitively keep related words close together. When a sentence gets long, they restructure to bring the verb closer to its subject or break the sentence into two.

rules.rule: Keep subjects and their verbs close together.
rules.guidance: 'The report, which was commissioned by the board in response to stakeholder concerns about environmental impact and prepared by an external consulting firm, recommends...' → 'The report recommends...' (move the modifying clause after the main clause or into a separate sentence).

rules.rule: Move heavy modifiers to the end of the sentence.
rules.guidance: In English, end-weighting is natural: put short elements before long ones. 'She gave the recently hired junior analyst who started last Monday the files' → 'She gave the files to the junior analyst who started last Monday.'

rules.rule: If a sentence feels hard to parse despite being grammatical, dependency distance is likely the problem.
rules.guidance: Re-read the sentence and ask: how far is the verb from its subject? How far is the relative pronoun from what it refers to? If the answer is more than 8-10 words, restructure.

dependency_proximity.research_basis: Muñoz-Ortiz et al. (2024) Section 4.1.6 demonstrates that all tested LLMs optimize dependency lengths to a lesser extent than humans. This aligns with the established DLM (Dependency Length Minimization) principle observed across human languages (Futrell et al. 2015).

cross_segment_variation.description: The most durable structural distinction between human and AI text: humans modulate their stylistic fingerprint between a document's sections (intro, body, conclusion), while LLMs hold one flat fingerprint throughout. This is a document-level property that sentence-level variety alone does not capture.
cross_segment_variation.ai_pattern: An LLM writes every section in the same register, with the same average sentence length, the same rhythm, and the same syntactic habits from first paragraph to last. Even when individual sentences vary, the per-section statistics barely move across the document.
cross_segment_variation.human_pattern: Human writers shift gears between sections. An opening might be terse; a middle section dense and clause-heavy; a close short and reflective. The variation across segments is itself a signal of a writer adapting to the work of each part.

rules.rule: Let each section read the way its job needs.
rules.guidance: Let each section's texture follow its job. A procedure can run short and plain while an argument runs longer and denser. Do not give a section fragments or questions just to make it differ. Applying any rule the same way to every paragraph re-creates the AI fingerprint at the level of the whole document. The checker flags this as segment_uniformity when ≥3 sections read alike.

rules.rule: Do not end every section on the same kind of beat.
rules.guidance: A common LLM tic is closing each section on a short, abstract copula maxim ('They are the product.', 'The second draft is the real one.'). Each is fine alone; as a per-section habit it reads as a machine landing every passage on a profound one-liner. End each section on its last substantive point, which is often a concrete detail.

section_types.instructions_or_tutorials: Clarity first. Short, direct sentences, and an even structure where the steps are even.
section_types.narrative_or_creative: Rhythm that follows the scene, with sentence length and word choice set by what each moment needs.
section_types.academic_or_technical: Domain terms used precisely and the same way each time. Sentences run longer where the reasoning is dense and plainer where it relaxes.
section_types.opinion_or_argumentation: A clear position argued from evidence. A question or a repeated phrase belongs only where the argument needs it.

cross_segment_variation.research_basis: Kuznetsov et al. (arXiv:2501.19301, EMNLP 2025): humans exhibit more variation across text segments than LLMs, which maintain a consistent stylistic fingerprint throughout. Its section_types carry what used to be foundation.section_level_variation. It is enforced by the segment_uniformity check in humanizer_check_text.
